title: Ruby tutorial: objects, blocks, arrays, hashes and classes — cv.cm
description: Learn Ruby in one page: run Hello world, variables and types, control flow, methods, arrays and hashes, blocks and iterators, classes, modules and exceptions.
answer: Ruby is a dynamic, object-oriented scripting language designed to be pleasant to read and write. Save `puts "Hello, world"` in `hello.rb` and run `ruby hello.rb`. Everything in Ruby is an object, even numbers and `nil`. The core ideas are methods defined with `def`, arrays and hashes, blocks passed to iterators such as `each` and `map`, classes and modules, and exceptions handled with `begin`/`rescue`.

sections.h: What Ruby is and what it is used for
body: Ruby was created by Yukihiro Matsumoto ("Matz") in Japan and first released in 1995, with the goal of making programmers happy. It became widely known through Ruby on Rails, the web framework behind sites such as GitHub and Shopify. Ruby is used for web applications, scripting and automation, and developer tools such as Homebrew and CocoaPods. Its standard implementation is CRuby (also called MRI).

sections.h: Install Ruby and run Hello, world
body: macOS and many Linux systems include a Ruby, but it is often old; install a current Ruby 3 with a version manager such as rbenv, asdf or mise, or with RubyInstaller on Windows. Check it with `ruby -v`.

body.code:
ruby hello.rb
# Hello, world
irb          # interactive Ruby shell

body: `puts` prints a value followed by a newline. Parentheses around method arguments are optional when the meaning is clear.
Variables need no declaration and hold any object. By convention names use `snake_case`. Constants start with a capital letter.

name = "Ada"
count = 7
puts "#{name} has #{count} items"   # Ada has 7 items
puts count / 2, count / 2.0         # 3, then 3.5

  puts "A"

  puts "B"          # B
else
  puts "C"
end

puts "pass" unless score < 50    # statement modifier

3.times { |i| print i, " " }     # 0 1 2
puts

n = 10
n /= 2 while n > 1
puts n                           # 1

kind = case "SAT"
       when "SAT", "SUN" then "weekend"
       else "weekday"

body: Blocks end with `end` rather than braces. Ruby code is usually indented with 2 spaces.
Methods return the value of their last expression, so `return` is often unnecessary. By convention, methods that return a boolean end in `?`, and methods that change the receiver in place end in `!`.

body.code:
def greet(name, greeting: "Hello")
  "#{greeting}, #{name}!"
end

def total(*nums)
  nums.sum
end

puts greet("Lin")                   # Hello, Lin!
puts greet("Lin", greeting: "Hi")   # Hi, Lin!
puts total(1, 2, 3)                 # 6
puts 4.even?, "abc".upcase          # true, then ABC

s = "hello"
s.upcase!          # modifies s in place
puts s             # HELLO

nums = [3, 1, 2]
nums << 5
p nums.sort, nums.first, nums.last   # [1, 2, 3, 5] then 3 then 5
p nums.sort[1..2]                    # [2, 3]

ages = { "ann" => 31, "bob" => 25 }
ages["cy"] = 40
ages.each { |person, age| puts "#{person} is #{age}" }
p ages.fetch("zed", 0)               # 0

user = { name: "Ann", city: "Oslo" } # symbol keys
p user[:name]                        # "Ann"

body: `p` prints the `inspect` form of a value, which is handy for debugging because it shows quotes and brackets.

A block is a chunk of code passed to a method, written with `{ ... }` on one line or `do ... end` across lines. Iteration in Ruby is done mostly through blocks instead of `for` loops, and the `Enumerable` methods make data transformations short.

body.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
p nums.map { |n| n * n }               # [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]
p nums.select(&:even?)                 # [2, 4]
p nums.reduce(0) { |sum, n| sum + n }  # 15
p nums.each_slice(2).to_a              # [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]
p %w[pear fig apple].sort_by(&:length) # ["fig", "pear", "apple"]

def twice
  yield
  yield
end
twice { puts "hi" }   # prints hi two times

body: `&:even?` is shorthand for `{ |n| n.even? }`. Your own methods receive a block and call it with `yield`.

body.code:
module Greeter
  def hello
    "Hello from #{name}"
  end
end

class Account
  include Greeter          # mix in module methods
  attr_reader :name, :balance

  def initialize(name)
    @name = name           # @ marks an instance variable
    @balance = 0
  end

  def deposit(amount)
    raise ArgumentError, "amount must be positive" unless amount.positive?
    @balance += amount
    self
  end

  def to_s = "#{name}: #{balance}"
end

acc = Account.new("Ann")
acc.deposit(30).deposit(20)
puts acc        # Ann: 50
puts acc.hello  # Hello from Ann

body: `attr_reader` generates getter methods. Modules group methods that can be mixed into many classes, which Ruby uses instead of multiple inheritance. The one-line `def to_s = ...` form needs Ruby 3.0 or later.

body.code:
def parse_age(text)
  age = Integer(text)       # raises ArgumentError on bad input
  raise ArgumentError, "negative age" if age.negative?
  age
end

begin
  puts parse_age("41")      # 41
  puts parse_age("abc")
rescue ArgumentError => e
  puts "error: #{e.message}"  # error: invalid value for Integer(): "abc"
ensure
  puts "done"
end

body: `rescue` catches exceptions, and `ensure` always runs. Inside a method you can write `rescue` directly without `begin`.

sections.h: A small complete program: word frequency

body.code:
path = ARGV.fetch(0) { abort "usage: ruby words.rb FILE" }

begin
  text = File.read(path).downcase
rescue Errno::ENOENT
  abort "file not found: #{path}"
end

counts = text.scan(/[a-z']+/).tally
counts.max_by(5) { |_word, n| n }.each do |word, n|
  puts format("%5d  %s", n, word)
end

body: Run it with `ruby words.rb notes.txt`. `tally` counts equal items into a hash, and `max_by(5)` returns the five entries with the highest counts.

body.note: Only `nil` and `false` are falsy. Unlike in Python or JavaScript, `0`, `""` and `[]` are all truthy, so test emptiness with `.empty?` or `.zero?`.

body: Start with the documentation page on ruby-lang.org, including the quick start "Ruby in Twenty Minutes", and use docs.ruby-lang.org for the core and standard library reference. Learn Bundler and gems for dependencies, RSpec or Minitest for tests, and then Ruby on Rails if you want to build web applications.

faq.a: Yes. Ruby on Rails runs many established web products, including GitHub and Shopify, and Ruby is common in scripting and developer tools. It is less common than Python or JavaScript for new projects, but it remains actively developed.

faq.q: What is the difference between Ruby and Ruby on Rails?
faq.a: Ruby is the programming language. Rails is a web framework written in Ruby that provides routing, database access and page templates.

faq.q: What is a symbol in Ruby?
faq.a: A symbol such as `:name` is an immutable, unique identifier. The same symbol is always the same object, which makes it efficient for hash keys and option names.
Both are good first languages with readable syntax. Python has a wider range of uses, especially in data science; Ruby is very expressive and is strong for web development with Rails.
